definition: STIT logic (from seeing to it that) is a family of modal and branching-time logics for reasoning about agency and choice.
details: A typical STIT operator has the form [ i s t i t : φ ] {\displaystyle [i\ {\mathsf {stit}}:\varphi ]} , usually read as "agent i {\displaystyle i} sees to it that φ {\displaystyle \varphi } ", and is interpreted in models where agents choose between alternative possible futures. STIT logics are used in action theory, deontic logic, epistemic logic, and the theory of intelligent agents to formalise notions such as "could have done otherwise", responsibility, joint action, and strategic ability in an indeterministic world.

explainer.lead: STIT logic (from "seeing to it that") is a family of modal and branching-time logics for reasoning about agency and choice. It matters for formalising responsibility, joint action, and strategic ability in intelligent agents.

tiers.eli5: It's a way of writing down rules about who made something happen and what else they could have chosen.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use STIT logics to model agents choosing between possible futures in action theory and agent design. A pitfall is that reasoning "from seeing to it that" holds only in models where agents' choices are properly defined.
tiers.paperLevel: A typical STIT operator has the form [i stit: φ], read as "agent i sees to it that φ", interpreted in models where agents choose between alternative possible futures; known limits are that the logic depends on the branching model and is used across action and deontic theory.

explainer.example: A designer writes [i stit: φ] to state that agent i brings about φ, then checks it in a model where i had alternative futures.
